claims.text: Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has relatively low hardness and compressive strength in its simple solid-solution state.
The low hardness and compressive strength of simple-solid-solution CoCrFeNiTi are caused by low lattice distortion and a lack of chemical short-range order.
Low lattice distortion and lack of short-range order permit facile dislocation glide in CoCrFeNiTi.
Slight compositional changes or thermal treatments can induce local chemical ordering in near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
Induced local chemical ordering enhances lattice distortion.
Chemical ordering and its associated local distortions impede dislocation motion by increasing local energy barriers resembling antiphase boundaries.
A B2-ordered Al28Co20Cr11Fe15Ni26 alloy deforms through heterogeneous slip of perfect screw superdislocations in its ordered B2 phase.
The disordered CoCrFeNiTi state has low solid-solution strengthening.
Facile dislocation glide explains the favorable ductility and machinability of simple-solid-solution CoCrFeNiTi.
Increasing short-range order in CoCrFeNiTi will raise hardness and compressive strength.
Increasing short-range order in CoCrFeNiTi will reduce plastic strain.
CrCoNi can be strengthened through a dislocation-triggered FCC-to-HCP phase transformation without compromising plastic deformation.
The proposed ordering mechanism applies only near the equimolar CoCrFeNiTi composition and in the absence of secondary brittle phases.
The proposed mechanism applies from room temperature through 600 °C under strain rates typical of compression and nanoindentation studies.
TEM or atom-probe tomography can be used to assess whether the intervention increased local ordering.
Failure of an ordering-promoted sample to show a statistically significant increase in both hardness and compressive strength relative to the baseline would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis predicts strengthening specifically when the intervention successfully increases short-range order, but the falsification rule also treats failure to confirm increased order as falsification. That outcome would instead indicate a failed manipulation and would not test the proposed causal effect of ordering.
The predicted outcome includes reduced plastic strain, but the falsification rule requires only increased hardness and strength and does not make the predicted ductility tradeoff decisive.
